background.definition: Rotator cuff disorder or impingement syndrome is characterized by shoulder pain due to inflammation in one or more of the muscles of the rotator cuff, including the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis. These are the dynamic stabilizers of the shoulder. It is also called subacromial shoulder pain.

list.listitem: A French study of workers in a broad range of occupations found the following prevalence of rotator cuff syndrome in men: 1.6% age 20 to 29 years, 4.7% age 30 to 39 years, 10.2% age 40 to 49 years, and 12.2% age 50 to 59 years.
In women: 2.7% age 20 to 29 years, 6.5% age 30 to 39 years, 12.7% age 40 to 49 years, and 15.1% age 50 to 59 years.
Overall prevalence: 6.8% for men, 9.0% for women.
Rotator cuff tears.
Subacromial bursitis.
Rotator cuff tendinosis.
The most frequently injured cuff muscle is the supraspinatus and its subacromial bursa.
Injuries to the rotator cuff are caused by either acute or chronic (overuse) events.
Acutely, irritation or tearing of the rotator cuff muscle(s) occurs in trauma from a direct blow or action against resistance.
Overuse rotator cuff injury occurs after repeated minor trauma to the cuff muscle(s); once a critical mass of inflammation outweighing repair is reached, impingement syndrome occurs.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Overhead athletes (engaging in baseball, tennis, swimming, etc.)

list.listitem: History can distinguish between acute injury and overuse injury and help to identify the cause, which can then be avoided. C
Lack of pain at night makes rotator cuff injury unlikely. B

Based on a Cochrane review, there is insufficient evidence for the accuracy of physical tests to diagnose shoulder impingements and disorders of bursa, tendon or labrum complicating shoulder impingement in the primary care setting. B
Overall clinical examination is 91% sensitive but only 54% specific for diagnosing rotator cuff tears. C
A clinical decision rule that includes three signs plus age can help diagnose rotator cuff tear. B
Ultrasound, MRI, and MR arthrography are all options for diagnosis of rotator cuff tears. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Relatively acute onset; full passive range of motion, but painful active range of motion; full strength
Subacute onset; less intensely painful, full passive and painful active range of motion; full strength
Depending on size; small: full strength; large: decreased strength
Decreased passive and active range of motion
Decreased active and passive range of motion; full strength
Status post trauma; large upper arm ecchymosis; weakness
Repetitive or irritant trauma; pain with flexion

list.listitem: History of acute trauma and/or sudden onset of pain will differentiate acute injury from overuse syndrome. Investigate work activity, sport participation, and the possibility of trauma as causes.
Rotator cuff tear is associated with a history of trauma (73% specificity) and is less likely in patients without pain at night (88% sensitivity).
The overall clinical examination will identify most patients with a significant tear, but it is nonspecific.

Specific physical examination findings that may be helpful include weakness on external rotation, supraspinatus weakness ("empty can test"), and signs of impingement (Neer or Hawkins-Kennedy tests). (See for guidance on how to perform these maneuvers.) However, all of these tests have limited positive and negative predictive value. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the accuracy of physical tests to diagnose shoulder impingements and disorders of bursa, tendon or labrum complicating shoulder impingement in the primary care setting.
MRI, ultrasound, and MR arthrogram are good imaging options for the diagnosis of full-thickness rotator cuff tears for patients with shoulder pain being evaluated for surgery.
Ultrasound at baseline, despite being able to detect bursitis and tears, may not predict outcomes at 6 months, based on a community-based prospective study.

With respect to detection of rotator cuff tears of any thickness, ultrasound, MRI, MR arthrogram, double-contrast arthrogram, and CT arthrogram were of similar accuracy. A Cochrane review found MRI and ultrasound to have similar accuracy for detecting any rotator cuff tear, but their sensitivities are poor for detecting partial tears, especially ultrasound.
MR arthrogram, compared to MRI, may be more sensitive and specific for full-thickness tears. However, MR arthrogram is more invasive, and should be reserved for specific clinical scenarios.
A clinical rule identified three independent predictors of rotator cuff tear: supraspinatus weakness, infraspinatus weakness, and impingement (see ).

A second clinical rule gave 2 points for age 65 years or older, 2 points for weakness on external rotation, and 1 point for night pain. Patients with 0 or 1 points had a 42% probability of rotator cuff tear, while 68% with 2 to 3 points and 91% with 4 to 5 points had a tear.
Suspect a rotator cuff tear in patients with nighttime pain, weakness on external rotation or supraspinatus weakness ("empty can test"), or signs of impingement.
MRI and ultrasound can help confirm the diagnosis.
Short-term use of NSAIDs and physical therapy are reasonable first-line therapies, considering the lack of certainty in the comparative effectiveness of various interventions. B
Subacromial corticosteroid injection only has modest, short-term benefits for rotator cuff disease. B
In those without full thickness tears, surgical decompression does not lead to long term benefits over placebo. A

Short-term use of NSAIDs, although poorly studied, is a reasonable first-line treatment, considering the lack of certainty in the comparative effectiveness of various interventions for rotator cuff disorder in adults.
Based on very low certainty evidence from a Cochrane review, topical glyceryl trinitrate may have modest, short-term benefits for patients with rotator cuff disorder with acute symptoms.

Subacromial corticosteroid injections have a small benefit over placebo, but do not appear to be better than NSAIDs. Any benefit appears to be short-term. Ultrasound-guided injections do not appear to be more effective or safer than injections guided by anatomical landmarks only.
For calcific tendonitis, ultrasounded-guided lavage with steroid injection is no better than sham lavage without steroid injection.

A trial enrolling 106 patients with rotator cuff disease treated in a physical medicine and rehab clinic in Norway found comparable short-term outcomes for ultrasound-guided subacromial bursa injection with corticosteroid plus lidocaine combined with gluteal lidocaine injection compared to ultrasound-guided subacromial lidocaine injection combined with gluteal injection of lidocaine plus corticosteroid.

Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections are no better than placebo and inferior to exercise therapy. A Cochrane review similarly concluded that PRP injection have uncertain benefits for rotator cuff disease.

A trial in Argentina randomized 100 patients with MRI confirmed supraspinatus tendinpathy refractory to conservative therapies to platelet risk plasma or corticosteroid injection. After one year, the visual analog score improved by 2.3 vs 1.7 points (p < .001) in the PRP group. however, a difference of 0.6 points is of borderline or no clinical significance.
Ultrasound-guided percutaneous lavage may improve pain, compared to extracorporeal shock wave therapy, but quality of the trials is low.

Botulinum toxin A injections may improve pain, shoulder function, and range of motion for patients with shoulder arthritis, based on very low certainty evidence from a single trial that was evaluated in a Cochrane review.

While many patients will undergo surgical repair of rotator cuff tears, the evidence base to guide treatment when comparing conservative therapy with surgical management is weak. It consists of small RCTs with varying definitions. The most recent Cochrane review and two other systematic reviews of RCTs found insufficient evidence demonstrating the superiority of surgery over nonsurgical interventions in terms of providing clinically meaningful improvements (eg, pain, function, quality of life).
The 10-year follow-up to the initial 2-year study (FIMPACT) found substantial improvement in all patients, with no benefit of surgery over sham surgery or physical therapy.
Another meta-analysis found small benefits to surgical repair, but many crossovers from conservative to surgical group.

A randomized controlled trial of 180 adults age 55 or older with non-traumatic supraspinatus tears found comparable outcomes in patients receiving physical therapy only; physical therapy plus acromioplasty; and physical therapy plus acromioplasty and rotator cuff repair after 1 year.

A randomized controlled trial of 313 adults found that investigational arthroscopy (i.e. sham surgery) was equivalent to sub-acromial decompression in patients without a complete tear. Both were only marginally better than no treatment.
A ten year follow-up study of a trial to compare surgery and exercise for rotator cuff tendinopathy showed equivalent outcomes between the two groups.
A ten year follow-up study of a trial to compare surgery and exercise for small and medium rotator cuff tears showed small benefits to surgical repair, which persisted at 15 years.

There is weak evidence to show that open rotator cuff repair is better than arthroscopic rotator cuff repair. However, a 2017 RCT of 273 patients in the UK found no differences in outcomes 2 years post-operatively. One small study showed that while an all-athroscopic repair had better short term outcomes than a mini-open repair, the long term outcomes were similar.
After surgical repair for small and medium tears, wearing a sling is probably not necessary. Pain is no different, and functional outcomes are slightly better without immobilization.
Meta-analysis of five studies found that functional outcomes with mini-open repair was equivalent to athroscopic repair of rotator cuff tears.

Traumatic injuries are more likely to occur in younger men (mean age 55 years) than degenerative injuries, and usually involve a fall on an abducted, externally roated arm. The tears are usually large and are generally surgically repaired. There was no evidence to guide early versus later surgery.

For pain control around surgery, limited evidence supports pre-operative gabapentin, perineural adjuncts (opioids, glucocorticoids, or α-2-adrenoceptor agonists added to the local anaesthetic solution) or postoperative transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation.
For shoulder replacement for osteoarthritis, reverse total shoulder replacement has similar outcomes to anatomical total shoulder replacement.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the effectiveness of shoulder replacement surgery for rotator cuff tear arthropathy.
There is not enough evidence to endorse or disprove the effectiveness of acupuncture. It may provide a short-term benefit.

Based on an older Cochrane review, there is insufficient evidence for physiotherapy for shoulder pain. A subsequent Cochrane review found manual therapy and exercise, based on one high-quality trial, to have comparable clinically efficacy to placebo. It added that the clinical benefits of manual therapy and exercise are likely similar to the effects of glucocorticoid injection and arthroscopic subacromial decompression, but this finding is based on low certainty evidence. Furthermore, manual therapy and exercise may increase adverse events more than placebo, but these events are only mild.
Exercises that involve flexibility and proprioception may be of more benefit than strengthening exercises for shoulder pain.
Scapular stabilization appeared equivalent to stretching and strengthening in one small trial (n = 30).
Thoracic spine manipulation, compared to sham, does not seem to improve patient outcomes.
The optimal "dose" of therapy for rotator cuff tendinopathy is uncertain.

Kinesio taping, compared to sham taping or other conservative therapies, has insufficient evidence for improving pain, function and range of motion among patients with rotator cuff disease, based on very low certainty evidence. It may improve quality of life, compared with conservative therapy, based on low certainty evidence.

Based on low quality evidence from a Cochrane review, therapeutic ultrasound may provide modest, short-term benefits for calcific tendinitis, while low‐level laser therapy (LLLT) may do the same for rotator cuff disorder. Pulsed electromagnetic field therapy (PEMF) does not appear to be effective, while the effects of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) are uncertain. These electrotherapy modalities do not appear to add clinically meaningful benefits to physical therapy alone. Finally, their benefits compared to active interventions (eg, corticosteroid injection) are very uncertain.

Radial extracorporeal shock therapy is no better than sham treatment for subacromial pain, although it may be better than placebo. A Cochrane review found shock wave therapy to only have marginal benefits for rotator cuff disease with or without calcification, based on low- to moderate-certainty evidence. Its safety is uncertain.
Most patients with rotator cuff disorder may improve with conservative management, but recurrences may be oommon. C
Degenerative, atraumatic rotator cuff tears that are small and among younger patients have more favorable outcomes compared to larger tears among older adults. B

A systematic review identified 9 studies regarding the prognosis of patients with traumatic rotator cuff injury. Traumatic injuries are more likely to occur in younger men (mean age 55 years) than degenerative injuries, and usually involve a fall on an abducted, externally roated arm. The tears are usually large and are generally surgically repaired. There was no evidence to guide early versus later surgery. B
Focus on pain relief, manual therapy, and exercises.
Surgery should be used as a last resort in patients for whom function and pain are not improved.

feature.caption: Specific Maneuvers for Diagnosis of Rotator Cuff Injury.a
feature.feature_body:
Test How to Do It
Neer test (impingement) Examiner takes patient through passive range of motion with internal rotation and forward flexion until 180°: test is positive with pain anywhere along arc
Hawkins-Kennedy test (impingement) Examiner takes patient through passive range of motion with internal rotation of the arm in 90° forward flexion and 90° elbow flexion: test is positive with pain
Lift-off test (subscapularis tear) Examiner resists patient's arm adducted and internally rotated and palm push-off in the central low back: test is positive with pain and/or weakness
Empty can test (supraspinatus tear) Have a seated patient abduct the arm to 90°, with 30° forward adduction. Then have the patient point the thumb toward the floor and resist downward pressure that you apply
Full-can test (supraspinatus tear) Examiner resists patient's abduction (thumb up) with the arms in the scapular plane and at 90° forward flexion: test is positive with pain and/or weakness
External rotation (tear) Have a seated patient flex the elbows 90° with the thumbs turned up. Then have the patient rotate internally about 20°. Finally, ask the patient to rotate the arm externally against your resistance
a See University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health for video demonstrations.
